metadata.description: The declarative NetworkManager desired-state for a host interface — addressing method, routes, DNS, and bond/bridge/VLAN membership — as a first-class estate record (DCM ADR-023). The body conforms to the NMstate interface schema by reference (Tier-2 adopt): UDLM owns identity + the version-pinned conformance pointer, NMstate owns the config body. Realized onto the host by a NetworkManager-family provider (a configuration-management engine, Kubernetes-NMState); maps 1:1 to Kubernetes-NMState NodeNetworkConfigurationPolicy.spec.desiredState. Supersedes bespoke per-tool host-network variables.

zone.description: WHAT KIND OF NETWORK THIS IS — DMZ, management, internal, storage — as a governed TAXONOMY term (Knowledge.TaxonomyTerm), not a property bundle and not a floor. A CLASSIFICATION, NOT A REQUIREMENT, and the distinction is why this is a taxonomy where `tier` is reference data: a floor is something a second provider can MEET, a category is something a thing IS. Taxonomy is also the only one of the two that carries `normalization_rules`, which is what this needs — providers report `dmz-2`, `DMZ_RESTRICTED` and `dmz restricted`, and all three have to land on one canonical term before any policy can match on it. FOR PLACEMENT ONLY (maintainer ruling 2026-08-10). Nothing critical hangs off a zone directly: it is not an authorization, not a control, and not a boundary. ANYTHING REQUIRED BECAUSE OF A ZONE IS ENFORCED BY POLICY READING IT — the model carries the classification, policy acts on it, which is the same split that governs everything else here. That also keeps the model on the right side of zero-trust architecture, which derives no trust from network location (NIST SP 800-207); UDLM already ships a `zero_trust.posture` setting that a location-as-trust reading would contradict. ON THE BASE though it does not apply to every network type (maintainer ruling 2026-08-10): enough of the family carries a category that the base is the right home, and an element that some types leave unpopulated is what `optional` is for. Scope IS portability (ADR-038 §3) — a category two providers can both report is portable by definition. Provider-reported, like `tier`.

tier.description: HOW GOOD THIS NETWORK IS — a reference to a governed `network_tier`, exactly parallel to `storage_tier`. Each term DENOTES A FLOOR (bandwidth, latency), so asking for a tier is asking for the floor and any network meeting it qualifies: one provider's "10G" and another's "high-throughput" are interchangeable iff both clear it. That is what keeps the intent portable — the match is against the floor, never the string. NAME-SELECTABLE BUT REQUIREMENTS-AUTHORITATIVE (ADR-036, ruled 2026-07-27): a consumer may select by tier name, explicit requirements win where both are given, and the provider records its native class as a realized output rather than something the consumer had to know. ON THE BASE, NOT A TYPE, because performance is expected to be consumable by ALL network class providers and portable (maintainer ruling 2026-08-10). Scope IS portability (ADR-038 §3), so the category base is where a fact every provider must report belongs. Provider-reported at registration or discovery — the party that knows is the one that says.

nmstate_schema_version.description: The pinned NMstate interface-schema version the `desired_state` body conforms to (the conformance pointer; NMstate releasing a new version does NOT force a UDLM schema change — the Tier-2 litmus).

desired_state.description: Opaque NMstate desired-state body — `state`, `ipv4`/`ipv6` (`enabled`/`dhcp`/`autoconf`/`address[]`), the type sub-objects (`vlan`/`link-aggregation`/`bridge`/`mac-vlan`), `routes.config[]`, `dns-resolver.config`. NOT restated field-by-field (adopt-by-reference); interpreted against `nmstate_schema_version`. 1:1 with NNCP.spec.desiredState.

applied.description: Whether the desired state is applied and matches on the host (Realized).

discovered_state.description: The NMstate current-state read back from the host; a diff vs desired_state is drift (OBS-001).

relationships.name: configures
relationships.description: configures — the adapter/port this profile applies to. Host-side declaration (dependent-side rule).

adopts.role: the whole config body by reference (Tier-2): state/ipv4/ipv6/vlan/link-aggregation/bridge/mac-vlan/routes/dns-resolver — NetworkManager declarative desired-state, 1:1 with Kubernetes-NMState NNCP

context.purpose: Captures a host interface's desired network configuration — addressing, routes, DNS, bond/bridge/VLAN membership — as declarative state a provider applies.
context.plain_description: What a host interface's network configuration should be, in NMstate's own schema: the opaque body is `desired_state`, interpreted against the pinned `nmstate_schema_version` it declares — the profile does not re-describe NMstate's fields. A NetworkManager-family provider applies it (a configuration-management engine, Kubernetes-NMState); the state read back from the host is published, and a difference between desired and discovered is drift. It replaces per-tool host-network variable files with one governed record per interface.
use_when: You need host interface config (static addressing, routes, VLANs on a bond) declared once and converged by automation.
You need drift in host networking detected from data, not by logging into hosts.
not_for: The interface device itself — Hardware.NetworkInterface; the profile configures a device that type inventories.
BIOS settings — Hardware.BiosProfile: the same opaque-body-plus-pinned-registry pattern, for firmware.
works_with: Hardware.NetworkInterface — the adapter or port the profile applies to.
Network.VLAN — the segments the configured VLANs and sub-interfaces ride.
